title: Reading in ragtime and eastern bands
summary: The reading versus aural-roots contrast, ragtime players like Chauvin and Turpin, and Bob Wright's ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, then this distinction then between the New York area being that jazz musicians playing more legitimately in terms of note reading and Louisiana being closer to the it's the aural roots of jazz or the shouting church and that kind of thing may not be a very valid one then.
Well, I don't know. I still think there's something to that
just if for no other reason judging from the records that we have. He also said ragtime was a lot of note playing and out of this
came out of this kind of thing you know those musicians.

Most of the ragtime players probably did read not all of them either. I think Chauvin didn't. I'm not sure if I ever heard that Tom Turpin did and there was a fellow that I recorded once Charlie Thompson who was quite a good ragtime player. He couldn't read but the tradition usually was I think that they could read and in order to play the complicated pieces and to do them accurately you would have to have either a sensational ear or be able to read those things to learn them very quickly. It would be quite a shower although there are some players Bob Wright I think learned 700 rags they claim and most of those he probably learned from ear. I'm quite sure he can read now too. I imagine he can. I've never even asked him.

A little while he played like Brunus for a certain stage in his life there in Chicago he got to be a Brunus fan and learned to play just like Brunus and that would have been done by ear too. But I remember when he was a kid I knew him when he was 10 years old so he would come down and play any rags that he'd ever heard and he didn't read those I don't think he had the music to them. He played them quite accurately too just a sensational ear that could do those things. But in general the ragtime players it was a note reading tradition I would say.
